title: Lyft | Connecting commuters to jobs | 2026
summary: According to our data, it seems more people are choosing rideshare to get to work. In 2025, one in three Lyft riders (37%) used rideshare to get to work, and in the first half of 2026, rides to work were 42% higher than they were in 2023.
body_markdown:
Picture the nine-to-five, and you’re probably picturing gridlock or a packed subway car, but that picture is changing. According to our data, it seems more people are choosing rideshare instead.


In 2025,[one in three](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15vzMQLAlSnv7mMK-XIuvcuEl88AmM447/view) Lyft riders (37%) used rideshare to get to work, and in the first half of 2026, rides to work were 42% higher than they were in 2023. Return-to-office trends don’t fully explain these trends, which[leveled](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/694361/hybrid-work-retreat-barely.aspx) out back in early 2023.


Bill Burns, who drives with Lyft in Portland, Maine, has a front-row seat to it. Most of his rides, he’s noticed, are people going to and from work — sometimes he’s taking the same rider from one job straight to the next. The data backs him up: Work-related rides in Portland have grown 43% since 2023. As Burns sees it, there aren’t many ways to get around the city, unless you have a car.


*“Bus routes are not terribly convenient or terribly reliable. They also don’t run on Sundays. So the question for them becomes, ‘How do I get to work?’” — Bill Burns, Top favorited Driver in Portland, ME*


The plot shows the eight-week rolling average of rides to workplace destinations, relative to the average from May 2023–January 2024 levels.


#### The transportation poverty trap


Cars are still how most Americans get to work —[nine out of ten](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/11/14/1-in-10-americans-rarely-or-never-drive-a-car/) U.S. workers drive. But not everyone has that option.[Eight percent](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/11/14/1-in-10-americans-rarely-or-never-drive-a-car/) of households don’t own a car at all, and 33% have just one. Among typical Lyft riders, that gap is even wider: 28% don’t have regular access to a vehicle. And of those riders, 52% have used rideshare to get to work — twice the rate of riders who own a car.


That gap tracks closely with income. Households[below](https://www.nationalequityatlas.org/indicators/car-access) the federal poverty line are four times more likely to be without a car than higher-income households. **19% vs. 5%** (below 200% of the poverty level, compared with above 200% of the poverty level). Lower-income households are 4x more likely to lack car access than higher-income households.


It adds up to a bind a lot of Americans know well: You need a car to get to work, but the cost of buying, insuring, and maintaining one puts ownership out of reach. Lower-income households are also more likely to live[farther](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/blogs/research-matters/2015/12/in-what-ways-are-d-c-area-neighborhoods-with-rail-transit-different-from-other-neighborhoods.html) from public transit, which only tightens the trap. Breaking out of it starts with one thing — a reliable way to get to work.


#### Addressing transportation barriers to employment


For the past seven years,[Lyft’s Jobs Access](https://www.lyft.com/lyftup/jobs-access) program has offered free and discounted rides to eligible job seekers — to interviews, to job training, through their first weeks on a new job — helping to remove one barrier between someone and a stable paycheck. Since 2021,[Jobs Access](https://www.lyft.com/blog/posts/job-access-program-500k-investment) has provided more than 135,000 rides to job seekers across 30+ markets in the U.S. and Canada.


*“Transportation shouldn’t determine whether someone can build a better life,” said Jerry Golden, Lyft’s Chief Policy Officer.*


We’re not doing this alone. Lyft and its riders’ ongoing commitment, through Round Up & Donate, help provide transportation access for job seekers via our longstanding partnerships with organizations like Goodwill and United Way. These funds provided almost $400,000 in free and discounted rides to job seekers in 2025 and are on track to exceed that total this year.


#### When riders commute with Lyft


Using the T-Index —[built](https://htaindex.cnt.org/download/data.php) by the Center for Neighborhood Technology — Lyft research found that the higher a region’s transportation costs, the more likely people are to turn to rideshare. The index measures the true cost of getting around: car ownership, everyday use, and transit. The pattern is clear — where transportation is expensive, more people turn to rideshare.


The figure shows the positive relationship between the 2022 T-Index (X-axis) and the share of rides in a county to workplaces (Y-axis, 2026). The T-Index, constructed by the Center for Neighborhood Technology, measures the burden of paying for transportation at the county level.


#### Rideshare matters most for low-income workers


Commuting with Lyft is growing fastest in low-income areas. Growth there took off around 2025 and has stayed 10 percentage points ahead of growth everywhere else. That tells us something important: For many lower-income households, rideshare commuting isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s essential.


The chart shows the growth in rides to workplaces by whether the ride started in a low-income area. Data presented as 16-week rolling averages.


Survey[data](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15vzMQLAlSnv7mMK-XIuvcuEl88AmM447/view) backs this up: In 2025, 45% of riders in households earning less than $50K used Lyft to get to work — nearly double the rate among riders earning over $100K.


**Cost comparison: Commuting by car vs. commuting by rideshare**


The cost of commuting via private vehicle is estimated for the typical American in 2026 and considers average 2025 gas prices.


Rideshare’s around-the-clock availability matters here too. Lower-wage workers are[more likely](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/atus.pdf) to work weekends, nights, and holidays — exactly when public transit runs least often. Our data shows it: Riders commuting to and from lower-income areas are more likely to be traveling on weekends and late at night, and more than 40% of work-related rides from low-income areas happen outside typical working hours. As Burns puts it:


*“Part of a community is ensuring that people can kind of get their basic needs met. Rideshare has become a part of that — enabling people who wouldn’t have any other option to get to work and live a dignified life through work.”*


The chart shows the share of rides to work that occur each hour of the week in 2025, by whether or not a rider is picked up in a low-income area.


#### Car ownership shouldn’t be a barrier to work


Not owning a car doesn’t have to mean being shut out of work — even if it sometimes feels that way. Plenty of traveling professionals, like travel nurses, get by without a car and still need a reliable way to their job. Burns sees this play out in Portland every day: “We need people to work as housekeepers, in hospitals, and at the grocery store, but some don’t have cars.”


With rideshare, people can skip the cost and hassle of owning and maintaining a car altogether — including the ones who’d otherwise be stuck in the transportation poverty trap.
